\begin{itemize}
\item DNB raised the buffer twice, to two percent, while the Basel indicator, the credit-to-GDP gap, pointed to \textbf{zero}.
\item The three boxes answer the three questions of the assignment: environment, criteria and risks, implications.
\item Our verdict: \textbf{normalisation, not tightening}. DNB refilled a buffer; it did not fight a boom. It cost banks little, was largely offset by cuts elsewhere, and we see no sign of a contraction in lending.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Announcements: May 2022 (1\%) and May 2023 (2\%); binding 25 May 2023 and 31 May 2024
\item Credit-to-GDP gap at the decisions: −33pp and −47pp → Basel guide 0\%
\item Inflation 11.6\% (2022) · CET1 17.7\% (end-2021) · €6.7bn releasable
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{CCyB:} Countercyclical capital buffer. Extra bank capital (0–2.5\% of risk-weighted assets) built in good times, released in bad times.
\item \textbf{Credit-to-GDP gap:} How far credit/GDP is above its long-run trend; the Basel starting point for the CCyB.
\item \textbf{O-SII:} "Other systemically important institution". The O-SII buffer is an extra capital charge on large banks.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 3/24 · March 2020\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:25 · from 1:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=3,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item March 2020: COVID hits. Within three weeks our neighbours \textbf{release} their countercyclical buffers so that banks can keep lending.
\item Sweden and Norway were at 2.5 percent; Denmark, Ireland and Lithuania at one percent.
\item The Netherlands was at \textbf{zero}. There was nothing to release.
\item France and Ireland followed on the first of April, and Belgium and Germany cancelled increases they had already announced. Across Europe, buffers built in good times were being used exactly as intended.
\item So DNB improvised. It cut the systemic buffers of ING, Rabobank and ABN AMRO and postponed a mortgage rule, freeing about eight billion euros.
\item DNB said this capital could support up to 200 billion euros of lending. But it was a workaround: these buffers were never designed to be released, so the cut had to be negotiated and explained bank by bank.
\item And it made a promise \emph{(pause)}: once things were normal, it would rebuild this capital as a two-percent countercyclical buffer.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Releases (rate in force → new rate):
\begin{itemize}
\item Denmark 1.0\% → 0\% (12 Mar)
\item Norway 2.5\% → 1.0\% (13 Mar)
\item Sweden 2.5\% → 0\% (16 Mar)
\item Lithuania 1.0\% → 0\% (31 Mar)
\item France 0.25\% → 0\% (1 Apr)
\item Ireland 1.0\% → 0\% (1 Apr)
\end{itemize}
\item Cancelled pending increases: Belgium 0.5\% (27 Mar) · Germany 0.25\% (31 Mar)
\item Also: Iceland 2.0\% → 0\% · Czech Republic 1.75\% → 1.0\%
\item NL: systemic buffers 3\% → 2.5\% (ING) / 2\% (Rabo) / 1.5\% (ABN AMRO); €8bn freed (incl. the floor postponement); up to €200bn of lending
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Release:} The authority lowers the CCyB rate with immediate effect, so banks may use that capital to absorb losses and keep lending.
\item \textbf{Systemic (risk) buffer:} A structural capital charge on large banks; not designed to be released.
\item \textbf{Mortgage risk-weight floor:} A minimum average risk weight on Dutch mortgages for banks using internal models.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "That empty buffer mattered, because not all capital can be released."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 4/24 · The releasable layer\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 1:00 · from 2:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=4,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Read the stack from the bottom: first the requirements banks must always meet, then the buffers on top.
\item The red dashed line is the MDA trigger. Below it, dividends and bonuses are automatically restricted. So banks avoid using buffers even when they are allowed to; in COVID, banks near that line cut lending instead.
\item The CCyB is different. The authority can switch it off, so the requirement itself falls and there is no stigma. It is the only truly \textbf{releasable} layer.
\item A release is also immediate, while an increase only binds after twelve months. That asymmetry is why the buffer has to be filled before the crisis, not during it.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Pillar 1 minimum 4.5\% CET1 · capital conservation buffer 2.5\%
\item CCyB 0–2.5\% of RWA (higher possible) · increases bind after 12 months · releases are immediate
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{RWA:} Risk-weighted assets. Assets weighted by riskiness (a mortgage counts less than a corporate loan).
\item \textbf{CET1:} Common Equity Tier 1. The highest-quality capital (shares, retained earnings), as \% of RWA.
\item \textbf{MDA:} Maximum distributable amount. The cap on payouts that applies once capital falls below the combined buffer requirement.
\item \textbf{Pillar 2 requirement / guidance:} The supervisor's bank-specific add-on (binding) / extra expectation (non-binding).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Two years later DNB refilled exactly that layer, at a strange moment."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 5/24 · The question\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:50 · from 3:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=5,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Now look at 2022: war, record energy prices, 11.6 percent inflation, ECB rate hikes and a housing market about to turn. And the Basel indicator says zero.
\item Under the Basel guide, a gap below two points means a zero buffer, and the gap was more than thirty points below that threshold.
\item Raising capital in a downturn amplifies the cycle, which is exactly what the CCyB is meant to avoid.
\item So our question: \textbf{was this the wrong moment?} We answer it in three acts, which are the three questions of the assignment.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item HICP inflation 11.6\% (2022) · ECB first hike 21 Jul 2022 (+50bp)
\item Credit-to-GDP gap −33pp (data to 2021Q4) and −47pp (data to 2022Q4)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Procyclical:} Policy that reinforces the cycle (tighter in bad times, looser in good times).
\item \textbf{Basel buffer guide:} Gap below 2pp → 0\% buffer; above 10pp → 2.5\%; linear in between.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Act 1, the setting. The refill followed a path promised in 2020."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 6/24 · Timeline\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:35 · from 4:15
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=6,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item After the promise in 2020, DNB published its framework in February 2022 and announced one percent in May 2022, just before the ECB began to hike.
\item In May 2023 it announced two percent, together with lower buffers for the largest banks. Both became binding on 31 May 2024.
\item It has held two percent every quarter since. The mortgage floor expires in November 2026.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 17 Mar 2020 · 29 Dec 2020 · 1 Jan 2022 · Feb 2022 · 25 May 2022 · 31 May 2023 · 31 May 2024 · 30 Nov 2026
\item ECB hikes: first on 21 Jul 2022; still hiking on 14 Sep 2023
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Announcement vs binding date:} Banks get 12 months between a CCyB increase being announced and having to meet it.
\item \textbf{CRD V:} The 2019 revision of the EU Capital Requirements Directive; it made the O-SII and systemic risk buffers additive, prompting DNB's conversion.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "By then the economy had fully recovered, but the outlook was darkening."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 7/24 · Macro\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:45 · from 4:50
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=7,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item By the third quarter of 2021 GDP was back above its pre-COVID level. That recovery is what DNB's framework requires before building the buffer.
\item Then came the storm: war in Ukraine, record energy prices, inflation of 11.6 percent and the ECB's first hike in July 2022. DNB warned that higher funding costs would strain debt sustainability.
\item So the macro picture argued \textbf{both ways}: build while the economy can take it, or wait because it is weakening.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item GDP above pre-COVID level: 2021Q3 (+1.9\% q/q) · end-2021 ≈ +3\% vs end-2019
\item HICP 11.6\% in 2022 (national CPI 10.0\%)
\item ECB +50bp on 21 Jul 2022
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{HICP:} Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, the euro-area-comparable inflation measure.
\item \textbf{Basis point (bp):} 0.01 percentage point; 50bp = 0.5pp.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "In the financial system, credit was cold and only housing was hot."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 8/24 · Credit and housing\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:55 · from 5:35
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=8,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Left: \textbf{housing was hot}. Nominal prices rose 19 percent in a year, and DNB itself called the market overheated. But as mortgage rates rose, real prices fell about nine percent.
\item In real terms prices were 16 percent above their 2007 peak, so the level was high even after correcting for inflation.
\item Middle: household debt is high, 107 percent of GDP against 58 in the euro area, but it was \textbf{falling}.
\item Right: the share of income spent on debt service was the lowest since 2005.
\item If there was a boom, it was in house prices, not in credit.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Nominal house prices +19.0\% y/y (2022Q1); real index 129 vs 2007 peak 111 (+16\%)
\item Real house prices −9.2\% (2022Q2–2023Q2)
\item Household debt/GDP: 110\% (2019Q4) → 107\% (2022Q1) → 100\% (2023Q1); euro area 57.7\% (2022Q1)
\item Debt-service ratio, households: 14.6\% (2022Q1)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Debt-service ratio:} Interest plus principal payments as a share of income.
\item \textbf{Real house prices:} Nominal prices deflated by consumer prices.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "And the banks entered this storm well capitalised."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 9/24 · Banks\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:45 · from 6:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=9,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Core capital was 17.7 percent of risk-weighted assets at the end of 2021, above the EU average, and in DNB's stress test the big banks stayed well above the minimum.
\item Rising rates also \textbf{lifted profits}: net interest income grew 6.7 percent in 2022. Remember that, because it comes back.
\item Act 1 in one line: war, inflation, rate hikes and a turning housing market argued against raising now; a recovered economy, cold credit and strong banks argued for it.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item CET1 17.7\% (end-2021; EU 15.7\% in 2021Q3) → 16.3\% (end-2022, in line with EU)
\item Stress test (FSR 2023): −3.8pp → 11.5\% at end-2025 (min. 8\%)
\item Net interest income +6.7\% in 2022; 67.7\% of bank income
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Stress test:} A simulation of a severe recession to check whether capital stays above the minimum.
\item \textbf{Net interest income:} Interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and funding.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ \textbf{\textcolor{nlred}{\textbf{HAND-OVER}}:} "That was the setting. So why did DNB ignore its own rulebook? Diego."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 10/24 · Why not the Basel rule?\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:30 · from 7:15
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=10,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Thank you. So why ignore the rulebook? Because on Dutch data it has a poor record.
\item The red line is the credit-to-GDP gap, credit relative to its long-run trend. We rebuilt it and match the official BIS series.
\item Under the Basel guide the buffer starts when the gap exceeds two points and reaches its maximum at ten. So everything depends on this one number being reliable.
\item It \textbf{missed} the financial crisis, at minus 13 in 2007. It raised a \textbf{false alarm} in 2012, during a bust. And it gets \textbf{revised}: 2016 read slightly negative at the time and plus 27 today.
\item The reason: Dutch credit grew from about 50 to 350 percent of GDP, and the filter mistakes that structural rise for trend.
\item One-sided means the filter only uses data available at each date, which is what a policymaker actually sees. That is why the signal can change years later, once new data arrive.
\item At the two decisions it read minus 33 and minus 47. The rule said zero.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Gap: −13.4pp (2007Q4) · +16.8pp (2012Q2) · 2016Q1 −0.6pp real time vs +26.9pp ex post
\item −32.7pp (2021Q4) and −46.8pp (2022Q4) at the decisions
\item Credit/GDP 47\% (1961) → 352\% (2015Q1 peak)
\item Replication error ≤ 0.00005pp (1971–2026)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{HP filter:} Splits a series into a smooth trend and a cycle; λ = 400,000 for credit cycles.
\item \textbf{One-sided vs two-sided filter:} One-sided uses only data up to each date (what policymakers see); two-sided also uses later data (hindsight).
\item \textbf{False alarm / missed crisis:} Type II / type I errors of an early-warning indicator.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "So DNB used its own compass instead."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 11/24 · DNB's framework\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:10 · from 8:45
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=11,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item DNB's 2022 framework has four phases: release after a crisis, \textbf{two percent in normal times}, more when risks are high, and release again in a crisis.
\item This is a \emph{positive neutral} buffer: already filled when risks are neither high nor low.
\item The two percent comes from history. Past crises cost Dutch banks about 12 billion euros at the peak. Two percent is about six billion of releasable capital, enough to support up to 150 billion of lending.
\item The ECB's own loss-based estimates give 1.1 to 1.8 percent, so two percent is at the top of that range but not outside it. We come back to that in the critiques.
\item Seventeen jurisdictions now work this way; Sweden, the UK and Poland also target two percent.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Peak accumulated losses €12bn (2007–2016) → 2\% ≈ €6bn → up to €150bn of lending
\item Build-up: 1pp per year → 2\% after two years
\item 17 jurisdictions with a positive neutral CCyB (BCBS 2024); ECB loss-based range 1.1–1.8\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Positive neutral CCyB:} A CCyB kept above zero in a "standard" risk environment.
\item \textbf{Peak accumulated losses:} The largest cumulative loss a bank suffered over a crisis period.
\item \textbf{Guided discretion:} Decisions informed by a published set of indicators, with judgement, not a formula.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "And its stated reasons were never credit growth."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 12/24 · DNB's reasons\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 0:35 · from 9:55
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=12,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item In 2022 DNB wrote that it was \textbf{restoring the buffers} it had lowered in March 2020, citing the recovery and a normal-to-elevated risk picture.
\item In 2023 it said the credit gap showed \textbf{no signs of excessive credit growth}, and pointed instead to risk appetite, falling property prices, debt sustainability and strong banks.
\item Credit growth was never the reason.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 1\% step: about €3.3bn of extra CET1 (announced 25/27 May 2022)
\item 2\% step: about €3.4bn (announced 31 May 2023)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Cyclical systemic risk:} Risk that builds up over the financial cycle (credit, asset prices, risk-taking) and can materialise system-wide.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "So what was the buffer meant for?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 13/24 · Risks and tools\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 0:55 · from 10:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=13,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Each risk got its own tool.
\item This matters for our question. If housing had been the target, the CCyB would be the wrong tool: it hits all lending, not just mortgages.
\item \textbf{Shocks nobody can forecast}, such as war, an energy shock, a sudden tightening or bank turmoil abroad, go to the CCyB, because it can be released whatever the source.
\item \textbf{Housing}, the known hot spot, went to borrower limits, tax reform and a mortgage risk-weight floor. The \textbf{size of the big banks} goes to the systemic buffer.
\item One instrument per target: the Tinbergen principle.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Banking sector: ≈ 400\% of GDP (when O-SII buffers were phased in) → 280\% (end-2022)
\item Risk-weight floor in force Jan 2022 – Nov 2026
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{LTV / LTI:} Loan-to-value / loan-to-income. Caps on mortgage size relative to house value or income.
\item \textbf{Tinbergen principle:} Reach each policy target with its own instrument.
\item \textbf{Borrower-based measures:} Rules on borrowers (LTV, LTI) rather than on bank capital.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "Now we can test the evidence against both readings."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 14/24 · The verdict\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 11:25
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=14,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Overheating or normalisation? Each predicts something different. Row by row:
\item If DNB was fighting a boom, the buffer should follow credit and prices. If it was refilling, it should follow a fixed path back to its normal level. These readings make different predictions, so we can test them.
\item \textbf{Indicators.} Overheating says the buffer rises with them. They all fell while the buffer rose.
\item \textbf{Path.} Normalisation says one point a year, then stop at two. That is exactly what happened.
\item \textbf{2023.} Prices falling, rates jumping. An overheating fighter pauses; DNB raised.
\item \textbf{2024 to 2026.} Prices up ten percent again. An overheating fighter goes above two; DNB held.
\item \textbf{Other buffers.} Normalising means cutting structural buffers in return. DNB did, twice.
\item \emph{(pause)} Five out of five.
\item Every observation fits normalisation, and none fits overheating. This is the core of our argument.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Gap, debt-service ratio and household debt ratio all falling in 2022–23
\item House prices +10\% y/y (DNB, Mar 2026) · CCyB held at 2\% since May 2024
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Phase 3 ("increased risk"):} The framework phase in which the CCyB goes above 2\%.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "And that last row tells us the refill was a swap, not a squeeze."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 15/24 · A swap, not a squeeze\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:00 · from 12:40
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=15,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item In euros, by our own estimate: the 2020 cut released about six billion; the CCyB then added 3.3 and 3.4 billion; the 2024 cut released another 2.7 billion.
\item Net, compared with before COVID, the requirement is roughly unchanged. DNB called it "more or less capital-neutral".
\item Two caveats: the bases differ, and compared with 2021 rather than 2019 it was a modest increase.
\item So capital was \textbf{moved}, from buffers that cannot be released into one that can.
\item Think of it as moving money from a locked savings account into a current account that the authority can open in a crisis. The total is similar; what changes is who can use it, and when.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item −6.0 (2020: ING 1.7, Rabo 2.4, ABN 1.9) · +3.3 (May-23) · +3.4 (May-24) · −2.7 (May-24 O-SII) → net ≈ −2.0 €bn vs pre-COVID
\item Valued at end-2022 total RWA; BNG excluded
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Structural buffer:} A capital charge for permanent features (size, interconnectedness), kept through the cycle.
\item \textbf{UK approach:} The UK offset its 2\% neutral CCyB by lowering Pillar 2A and resolution requirements.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "So, was it the wrong moment?"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 16/24 · The twist\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:00 · from 13:40
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=16,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item No. The storm made it the \textbf{cheapest} moment.
\item Headroom is capital above a bank's requirement. The four big banks had about 36 billion euros at the end of 2022; the full buffer of 6.7 billion is \textbf{at most a fifth} of that.
\item Bank by bank: Rabobank had 14.2 billion of headroom, ING 12.6, ABN AMRO 7.1, and even the smallest, de Volksbank, 1.7 billion. The first step of 3.3 billion was only 8 percent of the total.
\item And rising rates lifted profits, so banks could build the buffer from retained earnings instead of cutting loans.
\item ECB research agrees: profitable banks and a gradual build-up keep the costs low, also during the 2022 to 2023 tightening.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Headroom end-2021 / end-2022 (€bn):
\begin{itemize}
\item ING 16.9 / 12.6
\item Rabobank 15.7 / 14.2
\item ABN AMRO 7.9 / 7.1
\item de Volksbank 1.9 / 1.7
\end{itemize}
\item Total headroom €42.3bn / €35.5bn → CCyB €3.3bn = 8\%, €6.7bn = 19\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Headroom:} CET1 capital above the bank's requirement (its MDA trigger).
\item \textbf{Retained earnings:} Profits kept in the bank instead of being paid out.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ "And borrowers did not pay either."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred,colframe=nlred,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 17/24 · Borrowers\hfill\normalsize Diego Gutiérrez · 1:15 · from 14:40
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=17,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=nlred,colbacktitle=nlred!12,coltitle=nlred,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item We compare Dutch lending with five euro-area countries that never changed their buffer.
\item The controls are Austria, Finland, Italy, Malta and Luxembourg. They kept their buffer unchanged throughout, so any difference is not driven by their own policy.
\item The red line is the Netherlands minus those countries. The grey band shows the differences that arise by chance, when we pretend each control country was treated.
\item Mortgage rates stay \textbf{inside the band} at all three dates. Household credit grew \textbf{faster}, partly as catch-up.
\item In numbers: Dutch bank credit grew 16.6 percent from early 2022 to early 2026, against 7.9 percent in the euro area. Between 2019 and 2022 it had lagged, 4.3 against 11.3 percent. That is the catch-up.
\item So: \textbf{no sign of contraction}, though not a causal estimate. DNB reached the same view in September 2026.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Dates: May-22 (1\% announced) · May-23 (1\% binding, 2\% announced) · May-24 (2\% binding)
\item Bank credit 2022Q1–2026Q1: NL +16.6\% vs euro area +7.9\%; 2019–22: NL +4.3\% vs +11.3\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Event study:} Tracks the difference between treated and control groups before and after an event.
\item \textbf{Placebo test:} Rerun the analysis pretending an untreated country was treated, to see what chance alone produces.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=nlred!6,colframe=nlred!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{nlred}NEXT →}\ \textbf{\textcolor{nlred}{\textbf{HAND-OVER}}:} "So banks and borrowers were fine. What about the wider effects? Zheng."

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 18/24 · Monetary policy\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:35 · from 15:55
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=18,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Thank you. First, the buffer did not double the ECB's squeeze: Dutch lending rates moved with their peers, and bank profits rose with rates.
\item The ECB argues that building buffers early lets monetary policy focus on inflation.
\item With one monetary policy for twenty countries, the CCyB is the \textbf{Dutch-specific lever}, and insurance if a rate shock goes wrong.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item ECB hiking from Jul 2022 (first +50bp) to at least Sep 2023
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Macroprudential policy:} Policy aimed at the stability of the financial system as a whole.
\item \textbf{Monetary policy:} Interest-rate policy aimed at price stability (ECB, euro area-wide).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "Through reciprocity, the 2\% also reaches foreign lenders."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 19/24 · Across borders\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:30 · from 16:30
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=19,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item Foreign banks lending into the Netherlands must hold the Dutch two percent too, which limits leakage to foreign lenders. Leakage to non-banks remains.
\item And Europe is moving the same way: Germany, France, Ireland and Belgium raised their buffers in 2023 and 2024, and Portugal and Spain follow in 2026.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item Germany 0.75\% (Feb 2023) · France 1.0\% (Jan 2024) · Ireland 1.5\% (Jun 2024) · NL 2.0\% (May 2024) · Belgium 1.0\% (Oct 2024) · Portugal 0.75\% (Jan 2026) · Spain 1.0\% (Oct 2026)
\item Positive-neutral rates in 2023: Cyprus 0.5\%, Estonia and Lithuania 1.0\%, Ireland 1.5\%, NL 2.0\%
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Reciprocity:} Foreign banks apply the host country's CCyB rate to exposures there (mandatory in the EU up to 2.5\%).
\item \textbf{Leakage:} Credit shifting to lenders not covered by the rule (foreign branches, non-banks).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "The result for the Netherlands:"
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 20/24 · Resilience\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:55 · from 17:00
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=20,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item In 2020 the Netherlands had no releasable capital. Today it has \textbf{6.7 billion euros}, about half of past peak losses and enough to support up to 150 billion of lending.
\item It is cheap to hold and powerful to release: research suggests a release in bad times raises lending far more than the build-up costs in good times.
\item In numbers: a one-point build-up in normal times reduces lending by about 0.1 percent, while a one-point release in bad times can raise it by up to ten percent.
\item And with the mortgage floor expiring in November 2026, it matters even more.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item €0 → €6.7bn releasable · ≈ half of €12bn peak losses · up to €150bn of lending
\item Lang \& Menno (2023): −0.1\% lending per +1pp (normal times) vs up to +10\% per 1pp release (bad times)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{State-dependent effect:} The impact of a policy depends on the state of the economy (small in good times, large in bad times).
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "The price is reliance on discretion."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 21/24 · Critiques\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:50 · from 17:55
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=21,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Credibility:} without a rule, markets must trust DNB's judgement, so it has to explain itself every quarter.
\item \textbf{Calibration:} why two percent, when ECB estimates suggest 1.1 to 1.8?
\item \textbf{Untested:} will banks lend released capital, or hoard it?
\item In 2020 many banks did not use the buffers they were allowed to use. A released CCyB is different, because the requirement itself falls, but that has not yet been tested in the Netherlands.
\item \textbf{Baseline:} compared with 2021, it was an increase.
\item \textbf{Profits:} the same bank profits were also targeted by excess-profit levies.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item ECB loss-based range 1.1–1.8\% vs NL 2\% · +€3.3bn vs 2021 before the O-SII offset
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Rules vs discretion:} The trade-off between predictable formulas and flexible judgement (Kydland \& Prescott 1977).
\item \textbf{Excess-profit levy:} A temporary tax on bank profits seen as windfalls from higher rates.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\small\textbf{\color{navy}NEXT →}\ "In short, the promise was kept."
\end{tcolorbox}
\newpage

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy,colframe=navy,arc=2pt,boxrule=0pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]
\color{white}\bfseries\large Page 22/24 · Conclusion\hfill\normalsize Zheng Huang · 0:50 · from 18:45
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{1pt}
\fcolorbox{black!25}{white}{\includegraphics[page=22,width=\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax]{main.pdf}}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,width=0.585\linewidth,height=13.2cm,nobeforeafter,box align=top,fit basedim=13pt,colframe=navy,colbacktitle=navy!12,coltitle=navy,title=SAY]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Environment:} a recovered economy in a storm, cold credit, cooling housing and strong banks.
\item \textbf{Criteria and risks:} a two-percent normal level based on past losses, for shocks nobody can forecast, with housing left to other tools.
\item \textbf{Implications:} cheap, largely a swap, no sign of contraction, and 6.7 billion euros now releasable, at the price of discretion.
\item \emph{(pause)} In March 2020 the Netherlands had nothing to release. \textbf{Next time, it will.} The best time to fill a buffer is when nobody thinks you need it. Thank you.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.405\linewidth}\vspace{0pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=NUMBERS]
\begin{itemize}
\item 0\% → 2\% · −33 / −47pp gap · ≤ 1/5 of headroom · €6.7bn releasable
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}\par\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tcolorbox}[sbox,height=6.45cm,fit basedim=11.5pt,colframe=black!35,colbacktitle=black!6,coltitle=black,title=TERMS EXPLAINED]
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Normalisation:} Returning the buffer to its normal-times level, not reacting to overheating.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{minipage}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced,colback=navy!6,colframe=navy!50,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=2pt,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=3pt,bottom=3pt]

\begin{itemize}
\item Backup for method questions.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Credit gap:} one-sided and two-sided HP filter (λ = 400,000), plus Hamilton regression filter.
\item \textbf{Headroom:} (CET1 ratio minus requirement) × total RWA, per bank.
\item \textbf{Event study:} two-way fixed effects, three-month bins, placebo inference over five never-treated countries.
\end{itemize}
\item All references are verified.
\end{itemize}
